1198.title: Justice
1198.howItsDone: Christian moral teaching names justice among the cardinal virtues; churches teach it through paying fair debts and wages, giving thanks and respect, and working for the poor and overlooked, drawing on Micah 6:8 and the prophets.

segments.voice: Yesterday, prudence: practical wisdom, the right thing, the right way, the right time. Your line was wise in the moment.

Rent. A phone bill. A borrowed book still on your shelf. A friend who covered lunch last time. A teacher, years back, who believed in you before anyone else did and never heard you say so. Make a list of what you owe and it gets long fast, and only some of it is money. Christian teachers took up an old, plain definition of justice: giving each their due. Not revenge, not a courtroom drama. Just the steady work of making sure everyone gets what is theirs.

Paul comes close to that definition in his letter to the Romans: "Render therefore to all their dues: tribute to whom tribute is due; custom to whom custom; fear to whom fear; honour to whom honour." Taxes and fees, yes. But also respect, and honor. Some debts are paid in money and some in thanks, and Paul counts both. Proverbs adds the timing: "Withhold not good from them to whom it is due, when it is in the power of thine hand to do it." If you can pay it now, the delay itself is a small injustice. Then the prophets widen the frame from my bills to a whole society. Micah asks what the Lord requires, and the first answer is "to do justly." In Hebrew, that's to do mishpat, justice. Amos, as day 484 heard, pictures it as something that should never dry up: "But let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream." A river, not a single payment. Justice keeps flowing toward whoever is owed, especially the people easiest to overlook. And right after the list of dues, Paul says one more thing: "Owe no man any thing, but to love one another." Pay every debt you can, he says, except one. The debt of love stays open. You never get to mark it paid and walk away. Justice gives each their due. Love keeps on owing.

Let your mind walk slowly through your people and your week, a bill you've been putting off, something borrowed, an apology, a thank-you someone has never heard, and choose one debt, in money or in thanks, that it's in the power of your hand to pay. Hold it clearly. If you pray, you can ask for help to pay it.
Justice. Giving each their due, in money, in honor, in thanks. In the Hebrew of the prophets, mishpat.
Your line: each their due. The book on the shelf counts too. See you tomorrow.

1199.title: Courage
1199.hook: steady in hard things, neither reckless nor cowardly
1199.howItsDone: Christian moral teaching names fortitude among the cardinal virtues and among the gifts of the Spirit in Catholic teaching; some Christians pray for courage before hard tasks, and the story of Esther is read in churches and at the Jewish festival of Purim.

segments.voice: Yesterday, justice: giving each their due, in money, in honor, in thanks. Your line was each their due.

Queen Esther has a problem with a door. Behind it sits the Persian king, and the law says anyone who walks in uncalled is put to death, unless the king holds out his golden scepter. Her people are about to be destroyed, and she is the one inside the palace. Her cousin Mordecai sends her a message that ends with a question: "who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this?" Esther could stay quiet and safe. She could storm in. What she actually does is today's virtue, the one the old Latin lists call fortitude.

Fortitude is courage with its feet planted. Christian teachers describe it as a middle path between two failures: the coward who won't face the hard thing, and the reckless one who charges at it without thinking. Watch Esther walk that path. First, she doesn't rush. She sends word to Mordecai to gather her people and fast for her, and she and her maids will fast too. Then she says: "and so will I go in unto the king, which is not according to the law: and if I perish, I perish." That's not bravado. She's counted the cost and decided. And when she does walk through the door, she doesn't blurt out the whole crisis. The king holds out the scepter, and she invites him to a banquet. She chooses her moment: courage and prudence, working together. In the Bible, the call to courage can come with a reason attached. God tells Joshua, as day 697 heard: "Be strong and of a good courage; be not afraid, neither be thou dismayed: for the LORD thy God is with thee whithersoever thou goest." The courage isn't self-made. It rests on not being alone. And Paul writes to Timothy: "For God hath not given us the spirit of fear; but of power, and of love, and of a sound mind." Power and a sound mind, side by side. Steady, not wild. Jews read Esther's story aloud at Purim, and some Christians read it as a picture of a frightened person who walks through the door anyway.

Name something you've been avoiding because it scares you a little, a phone call, a hard conversation, a doctor's appointment, and instead of solving it, do what Esther did first: get still, and prepare. Plant your feet on the floor and picture yourself doing it calmly. If you pray, you can hold Joshua's words: be strong and of a good courage.
Fortitude. Steady courage in hard things: neither running from them nor charging in blind. One of the cardinal virtues.
Your line: steady courage. Esther went in not knowing how it would end. Back tomorrow, same hill.

1200.title: Temperance
1200.hook: enough, not too much: joy in good things rightly used
1200.howItsDone: Some Christians practice temperance through grace before meals, fasting seasons such as Lent, and moderation in food, drink and pleasures; some churches ask members to abstain from alcohol, while others drink in moderation and use wine at communion.

segments.voice: Yesterday, fortitude: Esther fasting first, then walking through the door. Your line was steady courage.

Honey. Proverbs has advice about it, and it's surprisingly practical: "Hast thou found honey? eat so much as is sufficient for thee, lest thou be filled therewith, and vomit it." No lecture about sugar. No claim that honey is bad. In fact the verse assumes you'll find some, and eat some. It just knows the moment when the next spoonful turns sweet into sick. Anyone who has finished a whole bag of something at midnight knows that moment too. Today, the last of the four cardinal virtues, the one that knows where that line is.

Start with what temperance is not. It isn't a suspicion of good things. A psalm thanks God for "wine that maketh glad the heart of man," and bread that strengthens the heart. Ecclesiastes says that to eat and drink and enjoy the good of your work "is the gift of God." And the first letter to Timothy says it outright: "every creature of God is good, and nothing to be refused, if it be received with thanksgiving." So temperance starts with yes. Good food, good drink, rest, screens, shopping, work: gifts. Temperance is the skill of enjoying them at the right measure, so they stay gifts and don't become masters. Paul lists it among the fruit of the Spirit in Galatians: love, joy, peace, and on through the list, ending with "meekness, temperance: against such there is no law." The Greek word there is enkrateia, self-mastery, being in charge of your own appetite instead of the other way around. The Book of Wisdom's list of four uses a different Greek word, sophrosyne, soundness of mind; the King James calls both temperance. And it's called fruit. Some Christian teachers speak of it as something that grows in a person, not a rule clamped on from outside. Churches apply it differently. Some ask members not to drink alcohol at all. Others drink in moderation and use wine at communion. Both are trying to keep good things in their place. Too much honey isn't more joy. It's less. Stopping at enough is how the joy survives.

Think of one good thing you tend to keep going with past the point of joy, scrolling, snacking, a show that rolls into the next one, and picture the moment it's good, then the moment it tips, the spoonful too many. Notice, gently, where that line sits for you. If you pray, you can give thanks for the good thing itself.
Temperance. Joy in good things at the right measure. In Paul's Greek, enkrateia: being master of your appetite, not mastered by it.
Your line: enough is joy. The good thing stays good when you stop. Twelve hundred days now.

1201.title: Pride and humility
1201.hook: pride, the root sin, is cured by humility, seeing yourself truly
1201.howItsDone: Some Christian traditions name pride among the deadly sins and humility as its remedy, and practice humility through confession, accepting correction and help, and serving others.

segments.voice: Yesterday, temperance: honey at the right measure, good things kept as gifts. Your line was enough is joy.

Naaman is a great general, honored by his king, and he has leprosy. A captive girl from Israel, a servant in his house, tells his wife there's a prophet back home who could heal him. So Naaman arrives at Elisha's door with horses and chariots and gifts. Elisha doesn't even come out. He sends a messenger: go wash in the Jordan. And Naaman storms off in a rage. He expected the prophet to come out, call on God, wave a hand over the spot. Our rivers back home are better than that one, he says. He's about to go home unhealed, because the cure was too ordinary for him.

Then his servants step in, and what they say is the whole lesson in one sentence: "My father, if the prophet had bid thee do some great thing, wouldest thou not have done it? how much rather then, when he saith to thee, Wash, and be clean?" Naaman listens. He goes down to the river, does exactly as he was told, and his skin comes back like a little child's. Notice who rescued him from his pride: a captive girl and his own servants, the people he least expected to need. Some Christian teachers treat pride as the root of the other sins. The Book of Sirach, in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles and among the King James Apocrypha, puts it plainly: "pride is the beginning of sin." And Proverbs adds where it leads: "Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall." But here's what's easy to get wrong. The cure isn't thinking you're worthless. Paul tells the Romans "not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think; but to think soberly." Soberly: not higher than the truth, and not lower either. Humility, in this picture, is simply seeing yourself truly: gifted and limited, capable and in need of help. Pride can't ask for help, because asking admits a limit. Humility asks easily. The letter of James puts it in one line: "God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace unto the humble." Some readers hear Naaman in it: the gift was there all along, waiting for him to stoop to the river.

Think of one thing you've been struggling with alone because asking felt like admitting something, a task at work, a repair, a heavy week, and name one person who could help, maybe someone you wouldn't expect, like Naaman's servants. Picture asking them, in plain words. If you pray, you can ask God for help too.
Pride and humility. Pride, which some Christian teachers call the root of sin, thinks higher of itself than the truth. Humility sees itself truly, and so it can ask for help.
Your line: see yourself truly. Not higher than the truth, and not lower. Until tomorrow.

1202.title: Envy and kindness
1202.hook: envy sours another's good; kindness enjoys it
1202.howItsDone: Christian teaching on the deadly sins pairs envy with a virtue that answers it, often named kindness or charity, and some preachers point to Jonathan's friendship with David and Paul's call to rejoice with those who rejoice.

segments.voice: Yesterday, pride and humility, and the help it takes to ask for help. Your line was see yourself truly.

The army is coming home. A young shepherd named David has just killed the giant, and King Saul comes home with him. Women come out dancing with tambourines, singing the kind of line a crowd chants: "Saul hath slain his thousands, and David his ten thousands." The text gives no sign anyone meant harm by it. But Saul "was very wroth, and the saying displeased him." Then one short sentence: "Saul eyed David from that day and forward." Nothing bad had happened to Saul. He'd won. Someone else had simply won more.

Envy is a strange sin, because it doesn't even get you anything. Greed wants the thing; envy can't stand that someone else has it. Thomas Aquinas, the medieval teacher, described it as sorrow over another person's good: their good news lands in you as bad news. The old Christian lists of deadly sins name envy among them, and Proverbs puts it in the body: "envy the rottenness of the bones." It eats from the inside, and the other person often never knows. Now look who else stands in that story: Saul's son, Jonathan. If anyone had reason to envy David, it was him. He was the king's son, next in line, and David was the rival for his own future. Yet "the soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul." Jonathan gives David his own robe, and his sword, and his bow. Later, when Saul is hunting David, Jonathan finds him in the wilderness and says, "thou shalt be king over Israel, and I shall be next unto thee." Father and son, the same news, two opposite hearts. Saul saw a threat. Jonathan was glad. That gladness is what Christians mean by kindness here: not just being nice, but being able to enjoy someone else's good. Paul puts it in one line to the church in Rome: "Rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep." For some, the weeping is the easier half. Celebrating a friend's promotion, the one you wanted, takes something else. That's the cure the tradition offers: not pretending to want less, but practicing being glad.

Choose one person whose good news reached you lately, a new job, a new baby, a win, and draft a congratulation in your head that stays about them: no "but", no story about yourself, no comparing. Try it once more, shorter and warmer. If you pray, you can say Paul's line quietly: rejoice with them that do rejoice.
Envy and kindness. Envy is sorrow at another's good; kindness, in Jonathan's way, is gladness at it.
Your line: their joy is mine. Their good news can be good news for me too. See you tomorrow.

1203.title: Wrath and patience
1203.hook: anger isn't wrong in itself; rage that wants harm is
1203.howItsDone: Christian teaching on the deadly sins names wrath, anger that seeks harm, and pairs it with patience; some Christians bring a grudge to confession or prayer, and some make a habit of settling a quarrel before the day ends, after Ephesians 4:26.

segments.voice: Yesterday, envy and kindness: Saul eyed David, and Jonathan gave him his robe. Your line was their joy is mine.

A prophet is furious with God. Jonah was sent to warn the great city of Nineveh, he finally went, and it worked. The people turned around, and God spared them. And Jonah is livid. Listen to why. He prays: "I knew that thou art a gracious God, and merciful, slow to anger, and of great kindness." That's his complaint. He's angry that God isn't angry. And God answers with one short question: "Doest thou well to be angry?"

Notice what God doesn't say. He doesn't say, never be angry. He asks whether this anger is doing well. That's the line Christian teaching draws: anger itself is not the sin. Mark's Gospel says Jesus once looked round on a room "with anger," and in the same verse, that he was grieved. Paul writes something close to permission: "Be ye angry, and sin not: let not the sun go down upon your wrath." So where's the line? The old teachers put it here. Anger rises at something wrong, an injustice, a cruelty, a lie, and that can be clean: the energy that makes a person stand up for someone. It turns into wrath when it stops wanting the wrong fixed and starts wanting someone hurt. When it rehearses the argument at two in the morning. When it keeps score. Paul's sunset is a deadline: don't carry it to bed. The answer the tradition gives is patience, and the Bible's phrase for it is the one Jonah threw back at God: slow to anger. A psalm says it of God: "The LORD is merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and plenteous in mercy." Proverbs makes it a kind of strength: "He that is slow to anger is better than the mighty; and he that ruleth his spirit than he that taketh a city." Slow, not never. The anger can still come; it just doesn't get to drive. James puts it in a sequence anyone can try: "swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath." Hear first. Speak later. Get angry last, if at all.

Bring back one small thing that made you angry this week, a driver, a reply, a tone of voice, and before doing anything with it, count ten slow breaths. Somewhere around six or seven, ask Jonah's question: is this anger doing well? If you pray, you can hold the psalm's words: slow to anger, plenteous in mercy.
Wrath and patience. Anger that wants harm, and the strength to be slow to anger, the way the psalm says God is.
Your line: slow to anger. Not never angry; just slow. Until tomorrow.

1204.title: Sloth and diligence
1204.hook: the monks' noonday demon: listless boredom with good things
1204.howItsDone: In Christian monastic tradition, acedia is met with stability and steady work: staying in one's place, keeping the hours of prayer, and doing ordinary tasks with care; the deadly sin of sloth in later lists grew from it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, wrath and patience: Jonah's fury, and God's question. Your line was slow to anger.

Midday in the Egyptian desert. A monk sits in his small cell. He came out here on purpose, to pray, to work, to be with God, and right now he can't stand it. He looks out the door at the sun. It hasn't moved. He looks again. Still hasn't moved. The day feels endless. He starts thinking another monastery would suit him better, or a visit to a brother would do him good, or maybe this whole life was a mistake. Nothing is wrong. That's the trouble. The old monks had a name for this hour, and this feeling: acedia.

Tradition says acedia is the old name behind the sin later called sloth, and it's a different animal from laziness. A lazy person might be happily asleep on the couch. Acedia is not happy. It's a heavy, restless boredom with the very things that matter: prayer, work, the people in front of you. Evagrius, a monk who lived in that desert and wrote about the thoughts that trouble monks, called it the noonday demon, and described that same monk staring at the sun, itching to be anywhere else. Some of the monks connected it with a line in the Psalms about a destruction that wastes at noonday. Noon fits. The morning's fresh start is gone; the evening's rest is far off. It's the long middle, where a lot of life is actually lived. The monks' cure was not a burst of effort. It was staying put. Stay in your cell, they said. Don't run. Do the next small thing with your hands: weave a basket, say a psalm, sweep. Scripture's blunt version: "Go to the ant, thou sluggard; consider her ways, and be wise." The ant doesn't wait to feel inspired. And Ecclesiastes: "Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might." Not the great task; the one in front of you. That's diligence: not hustle, but care that keeps showing up. Look back over this week and the same shape appears. Justice, courage, temperance, humility, kindness, patience, and now diligence: each a small, steady habit, practiced one ordinary day at a time.

Notice if there's a flat, heavy feeling anywhere in your day, a thing you keep circling and not starting, and don't fight it or plan to fix your whole life. Just name the next small task: one email, one dish, one page. If you pray, you can offer it, as the monks offered their baskets.
Acedia. The desert monks' word for listless boredom with good things, the noonday demon; the old root of sloth.
Your line: the noonday demon. The monks' cure was staying put. Same time tomorrow.
